body_markdown:
The *Mille Miglia* is set to celebrate its centenary in May 2027 with a six-day race around Italy.


First run in 1927 by Counts Francesco Mazzotti and Aymo Maggi, entrepreneur Renzo Castagneto, and journalist Giovanni Canestrini, the race was staged after the Italian Grand Prix was moved from Brescia to Monza. They devised a figure-eight looping route of 1500 km, or one thousand Roman miles, to Rome and back. Some 77 cars started the race, which Giuseppe Morandi won in his Officine Meccaniche 665 Superba in 21 hours, four minutes and 48 seconds, despite torrential downpours, fog and dust clouds disrupting the drive.


In the fastest-ever race of 1955, Stirling Moss and Denis Jenkinson famously used pace notes to help them complete the route in a stunning 10 hours, seven minutes and 48 seconds. Their[Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-holy-grail-what-makes-the-300-slr-coupe-so-valuable/) averaged 97.96 mph.


Mille crowds and a 300-horse, open-piped, straight-eight Mercedes at full yawp.


Getty Images


Taking place on public roads, the *Mille Miglia* would become notorious as one of the most dangerous races in history, with 56 people killed in 30 years—more than half of which were spectators. It was cancelled after the 1957 event, which saw Spain’s Alfonso de Portago and American navigator Edmund Nelson killed in their Ferrari, alongside nine spectators.


In 1977, the race returned as a regularity trial, which meant that the 300 cars entered wouldn’t be racing flat out, but would be competing to get closest to a calculated time over the 1000 miles. The same format has been kept ever since, but with a variety of different route variations.


To mark the *Mille Miglia’* s 100th anniversary, the 2027 event will follow a similar path to the original, leaving Brescia for Parma on May 24, then to Modena over the[Raticosa](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/on-the-road-in-the-mc20-maseratis-most-sophisticated-supercar/) and Futa Passes to Florence on day two. Day three will dispatch the drivers through the Chianti Valley to Arezzo and Siena, and onwards to Rome. Then it’s south again to Perugia, Gradara, and Cervia for the fourth day. Day five passes through Ferrara, Ravigo, and Padua before reaching Verona. Then it’s the final leg back to Brescia’s Viale Venezia for prizes and a party.


“Reaching the historic milestone of one hundred years is a source of immense pride for the Automobile Club Brescia and for our entire community,” says Aldo Bonomi, President of the Automobile Club of Brescia. “The *Mille Miglia* is the ultimate expression of ingenuity, courage and that typically Brescian know-how, which, a century ago, gave rise to a legendary endeavor.”


The event is only open to classic cars of which an example took part in one of the first 30 years of the Mille Miglia from 1927 to 1957. They must also be recorded on the[Mille Miglia Register.](https://www.registro1000miglia.it/) Over 400 cars are expected to enter, with[registration opening](https://1000miglia.it/en/) on October 6.
